content: The MORN repeat-containing 1 (MORN1) protein, also referred to as Morn1, is encoded by the MORN1 gene in humans. The precise biological function of MORN1 remains poorly understood. Orthologs of this protein have been identified in both eukaryotes and bacteria. The MORN1 protein contains seven MORN repeats and is encoded by a gene comprising 1641 base pairs distributed across 14 exons in the reference mRNA transcript. On the minus strand of the genome, the PEX10 gene is located upstream of the MORN1 gene. Alternative Splicing The MORN1 gene contains 19 distinct GT-AG introns and produces 15 different mRNA transcripts. Of these, 11 are generated through alternative splicing, while 4 remain unspliced. Among these variants, there are 4 probable alternative promoters, 9 non-overlapping alternative last exons, and 6 alternative polyadenylation sites. Additionally, 753 base pairs of the MORN1 gene are antisense to the spliced SKI gene, and 193 base pairs are antisense to the RER1 gene. These antisense regions may play a role in regulating the expression of MORN1 itself or its neighboring genes. Protein Characteristics The MORN1 gene encodes a protein consisting of 497 amino acids. This protein contains two overlapping conserved domains. The first domain is the MORN repeat region, which includes seven MORN repeats located between residues 38 and 211, classified under the protein family pfam02493. The second domain is a multidomain conserved protein found in bacteria (COG4642), which encompasses the MORN repeat region and the initial target sequence (residues 1–211). The remaining 286 amino acids are less conserved among orthologs, particularly distant ones, and do not belong to any known protein family. The MORN1 protein lacks long hydrophobic regions, suggesting it is not a transmembrane protein. It is predicted to localize in the cytoplasm, nucleus, or mitochondria. Although the genomic context does not necessarily indicate function, MORN1 is predicted to contain a second peroxisomal targeting signal at residues 451 (sequence: RLPPAFKHL), which may suggest interactions with the PEX10 protein. Additionally, a nuclear export signal has been predicted near the C-terminal end of the protein at residues 334–338 (sequence: LELH), located in a non-MORN repeat-containing region. Post-Translational Modifications The MORN1 protein is predicted to undergo several post-translational modifications. Glycosylation sites have been identified at serine 488 and threonine residues. Conserved serine, tyrosine, and threonine residues have also been predicted as phosphorylation sites, which are conserved among orthologs. MORN Repeats The MORN (Membrane Occupation and Recognition Nexus) repeat is a structural motif found in multiple copies across various proteins, including junctophilins. A MORN-repeat protein has been identified in the parasite Toxoplasma gondii and other apicomplexan protists. In T. gondii, MORN1 plays a critical role in nuclear division and daughter cell budding. It is specifically associated with spindle poles, as well as the anterior and interior rings of the inner membrane complex during asexual and sexual reproduction, budding, and schizogony. Overexpression of MORN1 in T. gondii results in severe defects in nuclear segregation and daughter cell formation. The MORN repeats are not identical but follow a general pattern, beginning with a YEG sequence. The subsequent glycine residues are highly conserved, even among microbial orthologs, suggesting their importance in the structural or functional role of the protein. Tissue Distribution Expression data from expressed sequence tags (ESTs) and microarrays indicate that MORN1 is predominantly expressed in the brain, eyes, lungs, parathyroid, salivary glands, testes, kidneys, and trachea. It is also expressed to a lesser extent in the ovaries, prostate, thymus, and trachea. MORN1 is expressed in both adult and fetal tissues. In terms of health states, MORN1 is expressed in normal tissues as well as in germ cell and kidney tumors. Orthologs Orthologs of the MORN1 protein have been identified in mammals and invertebrates. However, reptiles, insects, and birds show limited conservation of this protein. Bacteria and protists exhibit a level of conservation similar to that observed in birds and reptiles, despite being evolutionarily more distant from humans. Structural Similarity Based on C-BLAST analysis, MORN1 shares sequence similarity with Chain A of the histone methyltransferase Set7/9. Specifically, MORN1 aligns with 77 amino acids of this chain, spanning residues 81–158.
